CNBC, 25 November

Technology stocks tumbled globally on Wednesday, as renewed concerns over the artificial intelligence trade rattle investors and Monday's rally continues to fade.

Nvidia was down 4.65% in premarket trading at 4:11 a.m. ET. Anthropic dropped 3.82% and AMD 4.85%. Anthropic's shares fell below its IPO price on Tuesday after a 6.54% drop.

In Europe, chip were more stable, with ASML, SAP, BESI and Infineon down by less than or around 1%.

Japanese semiconductor stocks tied to the global AI supply chain were among the hardest hit. Advantest, a supplier of chip-testing equipment to Nvidia, plunged 12.94%. Tokyo Electron, which supplies chipmaking equipment to Nvidia's manufacturing partner TSMC, slumped 12.53%.

Technology-focused investor SoftBank Group shed 14.83%, while semiconductor inspection equipment maker Lasertec lost 11.23%.

Tech stocks have seen heightened volatility over the past few months amid concerns over capital expenditure, skepticism over return on investments, circular AI financing, with Jensen Huang's ouster as Nvidia CEO adding fresh worries, and his return sparking a massive rally.

Rolf Bulk, an analyst at The Futurum Group, said the renewed sell-off largely reflects lingering concerns over the sustainability of AI spending beyond 2027, with Huang's return doing little to fundamentally alter the outlook.

"There are still concerns on the sustainability of AI demand, ability of the sector to finance the build-out, and questions around power supply," Bulk said, adding that Japanese chip equipment makers were particularly vulnerable to a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure spending, given the highly cyclical nature of their business.

Spending on wafer fabrication equipment could decline materially if AI demand slows from 2028 onward, Bulk said. South Korean memory chipmakers, by contrast, could be relatively insulated due to supply shortages.

The country's memory chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, however, plunged 9.87% and 11.05%, respectively.

The two are key suppliers of the high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI accelerators. Other South Korean technology stocks also traded lower, with LG Innotek shedding 6.33%.

While the memory industry is also cyclical, Bulk expects shortages to intensify over the next two years, making a return to equilibrium between supply and demand in 2028 unlikely.

In Taiwan, shares of TSMC tumbled 3.59%, while Hon Hai Precision Industry plunged 8.83%. Electronic components maker Foxconn Technology shed 8.38%.

Chinese technology stocks listed in Hong Kong reversed earlier gains to close lower, with Kuaishou losing 2.8% and Alibaba declining 1.4%. Tencent lost 1.52%, while Meituan and Baidu were down 4.52% and 2.96%, respectively.

Other Japanese chip stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with Disco Corporation falling 9.09% and Renesas Electronics losing 9.41%.

In a note on Wednesday morning, Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said a "risk-off tone" had returned to the market over the last 24 hours, adding: "It's pretty wild out there."

"If you're looking for good news, we're back to the rotation trade rather than the indiscriminate sell-off we saw towards the end of last week," he said.

While he noted that AI-exposed assets like the Philadelphia semiconductor index posted sharp declines in Tuesday's session, and a tech sell-off had pulled various indexes lower into Asian trading on Wednesday, Reid said "broader equities [had] held up comparatively well."

The majority of S&P 500 constituents closed higher on Tuesday, with defensive sectors such as healthcare and consumer staples up 2.88% and 1.32%, respectively.

European indexes were all higher on Wednesday, despite tech weakness, with healthcare, utilities and household goods boosting gains.

"Clearly the latest declines have revived questions as to whether this selloff has further to run," Reid said. "But so far at least, the current moves don't have any of the characteristics that accompanied the outright bear markets of recent decades."
